claims.text: Chemical short-range order suppresses lattice thermal conductivity in concentrated refractory high-entropy alloys relative to a fully random solid solution.
SRO enhances phonon scattering through SRO-induced local strain fields.
Local bond-stiffness heterogeneity associated with SRO reduces phonon group velocities.
MoNbTaW can exhibit a significant energetic driving force for chemical short-range ordering.
High-temperature homogenization followed by rapid quenching produces a fully random MoNbTaW state with negligible SRO.
Moderate-temperature annealing can induce SRO in a refractory HEA without producing long-range order or phase separation.
Annealing between 0.4 and 0.6 times the melting temperature is an appropriate window for establishing steady-state SRO in the proposed RHEA.
Rapid quenching after annealing preserves the anneal-induced SRO during room-temperature characterization and subsequent thermal measurements.
A non-random atomic distribution creates local lattice distortions and spatially fluctuating force constants.
SRO-related distortions and force-constant fluctuations scatter mid-to-long-wavelength phonons more effectively than the fully random configuration.
SRO can reduce local mass-variance fluctuations relative to a random alloy.
In refractory alloys, correlated strain fields and bond-stiffness variations dominate over the reduction in mass-fluctuation scattering.
SRO correlations act as resonant or strong phonon-scattering centers, particularly when phonon wavelengths are comparable to the SRO correlation length.
SRO shortens phonon mean free paths relative to a random alloy in which compositional scattering is stochastic.
The SRO-containing alloy will have lower lattice thermal conductivity than the random alloy from 300 to 1000 K.
The conductivity suppression will be greatest from 300 to 600 K because phonon-phonon scattering is less dominant there than defect or structural scattering.
The proposed suppression requires sufficiently large atomic-size mismatch and elastic-modulus differences to create strong local strain fields upon ordering.
Chemical ordering can drive multicomponent alloys from disordered solid solutions toward ordered, intermetallic, or multiphase structures.
Long-range superlattice formation may change thermal transport through band gaps or coherent interfaces rather than through the proposed SRO-scattering mechanism.
If SRO is too weak to alter the phonon-scattering cross-section appreciably, it will not produce the predicted conductivity suppression.
